<problem>
A finite set $A\subset\mathbb N$ is a Sidon set if the differences $a-a'$ with $a\neq a'$, $a,a'\in A$, are pairwise distinct. A finite set $B\subset\mathbb Z$ whose elements are pairwise distinct modulo $v\ge 1$ is a perfect difference set modulo $v$ if every nonzero residue class modulo $v$ equals $b-b'$ for exactly one ordered pair of distinct $b,b'\in B$. Say $A$ extends if $A\subseteq B$ for some $v\ge1$ and some perfect difference set $B$ modulo $v$. For $k,N\in\mathbb N$ let $S_k(N)$ be the number of $k$-element Sidon subsets of $[N]=\{1,\dots,N\}$ and $E_k(N)$ the number of those that extend, and put $c_k=\limsup_{N\to\infty}E_k(N)/S_k(N)\in[0,1]$. (1) Is $c_k<1$ for some $k$, and does $c_k\to0$ as $k\to\infty$? (2) Is $E_4(N)=S_4(N)$ for all $N$, i.e. does every Sidon set with at most four elements extend?
</problem>

<solution>
Answers (not proved): (1) Yes, and yes. I expect $c_k<1$ for some $k$ (I expect $k=5$ already) and $c_k\to0$. (2) Yes. I expect every Sidon set with at most four elements to extend. These rest on a heuristic count, on a lemma I proved, and on a counterexample I am recalling from the literature but did not re-derive. Nothing below proves either part.

1. Proved lemma: sums in a perfect difference set are almost unique. Let $B$ be a perfect difference set mod $v$ and suppose $b_1+b_2\equiv b_3+b_4$ with all $b_i\in B$. Then $b_1-b_3\equiv b_4-b_2$. Since each nonzero difference comes from exactly one ordered pair, either $b_1=b_3$ or $b_1=b_4$. So each residue $s$ is $b+b'$ for at most one unordered pair $\{b,b'\}$ ($b=b'$ allowed). Consequences: $-B$ meets every translate $B+t$ in at most 2 points (it is an oval in the cyclic projective plane). If $x,2x,4x\in B$ then $0\notin B$, since otherwise $0+2x=x+x$ gives two representations of one sum.

2. Known obstructions (recalled, not re-derived). A perfect difference set with $|B|=n+1$ has $v=n^2+n+1$. M. Hall (1947) showed $\{1,3,9,10,13\}$ does not extend. Alexeev–Mixon (2025, Lean-verified) showed $\{1,2,4,8,13\}$ does not extend. Either example shows not every Sidon set extends. But $c_5<1$ needs more: a positive proportion of 5-element Sidon sets must fail to extend.

3. Heuristic count. Take Singer difference sets $B_q$ of prime-power order $q$, $v=q^2+q+1$, and $A=\{0,x_2,\dots,x_k\}$ (after translation). For a dilation $t\in(\mathbb Z/v)^*$ we need a base point $b$ with $b+tx_i\in B_q$ for all $i$. The condition for $x_2$ fixes $b$ uniquely, because $|B_q\cap(B_q-tx_2)|=1$. Each of the other $k-2$ conditions then holds with probability about $|B_q|/v\approx1/q$. Up to the multiplier group (size $3\log_p q$) there are about $q^2/\log q$ essentially different dilations. So the expected number of embeddings is about $q^{4-k}/\log q$. Summing over prime powers $q$:
- $k\le4$: the sum diverges, so a generic 4-element Sidon set should embed for infinitely many $q$ (for $k=3$ there is huge slack). This supports (2).
- $k=5$: $\sum 1/(q\log q)$ over prime powers converges, so a positive proportion of 5-sets should embed in no Singer set. If no other perfect difference sets exist (the prime-power conjecture), a positive proportion fails to extend, giving $c_5<1$.
- Large $k$: the expected count is dominated by small $q$ and, for a typical set in $[N]$, tends to $0$ as $k\to\infty$, giving $c_k\to0$.

What remains to make this rigorous: (a) for $c_k<1$ and $c_k\to0$, an argument valid for perfect difference sets of every order $n$, not only Singer sets (e.g. via the multiplier theorem or the oval structure in step 1), or an obstruction like $\{1,2,4,8,13\}$ that survives small perturbations and so covers a positive proportion of $k$-sets; (b) for (2), an explicit embedding of every 4-element Sidon set into some Singer set, which needs a second-moment or character-sum version of the count in step 3.
</solution>
